modules.doc: Localization: one `strings/<locale>.toml` per language, keys to strings. `[locale]` in `project.toml` sets the starting locale, the fallback and the locales written right to left (`right_to_left`); a key neither has comes back as itself.

docs.locales: Every locale the project ships a `strings/<locale>.toml` for, in name order.
docs.right_to_left: Whether the locale in force is written right to left: its language is in `[locale] right_to_left`, which starts as Arabic, Sorani, Dhivehi, Persian, Hebrew, Pashto, Sindhi, Uyghur, Urdu and Yiddish. A UI in one lays out mirrored: rows run from the right, start and end swap, and an icon its theme lists under `[icons] mirrored` turns round.
docs.set_locale: Switch locale; the next `tr` answers in it, which for a widget showing a key is the next frame.
docs.system_locale: The locale the operating system reports, like `en-US`, or nil when it says nothing; recorded with the session. A run starts in the shipped locale nearest it unless `[locale] initial` says.
docs.tr: The string for a key in the current locale. `{name}` in it is replaced by the argument called `name`, and an `n` argument also picks the plural form the locale's language calls for.

modules.name: strings

modules.doc: Waiting inside an async method: `init` and event handlers may await; `update` is synchronous.

docs.frames: Park an async method for a number of fixed steps; counted on the tick, so a replay waits exactly as long.
docs.seconds: Park an async method for a span of simulation time, woken on fixed step `ceil(seconds * tick_hz)`, so 4/60 at 60 Hz is 4 steps; the wall clock never enters it.
docs.wait: Park an async method until the engine wakes the token a binding gave it, and answer what it woke with. An answer that came first is kept until a wait takes it, or the node that asked for it is freed.

modules.name: task

modules.doc: TOML text to and from script tables, the format of scene files, asset definitions and component properties.

docs.encode: A table written back out as TOML text; a node or callback in it is not data and is an error.
docs.parse: The table a TOML document describes; nil for text that does not parse.
docs.patch: The document's text with this table's keys written into it, keeping every comment, the key order and any table the value does not name. What a tool saving a hand-written file uses instead of `encode`.

modules.name: toml

modules.doc: The names of a value's type: what `kind()` answers on an `any`.
modules.name: types

modules.doc: What a script asks of the UI and tells it: where a `widget` node drew, focus, the screen's classes, the scale, the theme, the clipboard, when a pass runs and the control tables a form writes. Nothing here draws; a UI is `widget` nodes in a scene.

docs.chord_text: A chord as a widget's `shortcut` and `[input.actions]` spell it, `cmd+shift+KeyS`, in the spelling the platform shows: `⇧⌘S` on a Mac, `Ctrl+Shift+S` elsewhere. What a row naming a command writes beside it. A chord no key reads is an error.
docs.clear_focus: Focus nothing, as a pad's back button leaves a menu; the widget focus leaves hears `focus_exited`, and a field being typed into lets the keyboard go. A focused widget hidden or freed gives its focus up on its own, a field its keyboard too.
docs.click: Click a widget node as the pointer would, at the next tick and with no window needed: what a test harness drives the game with. False for a node a pointer could not click, hidden, disabled or not a widget; `{ hidden: true }` clicks a hidden one anyway, as a test emitting its signal would, and `{ at: Vec2 }` lands on a `view` there, in the window's design pixels, which it says as `view_clicked`.
docs.colors_apart: Every pair of a `widget_theme` document's colours that say something by hue (`primary`, `success`, `warning`, `danger`), closest first, as `{ first, second, distance, vision }`: how far apart they stand in CIELAB for the colour vision that sees them closest. Under 10 the two read as one colour to that reader.
docs.complete_theme: The theme document with every colour and size it leaves out derived from its sources, and `dark` stated.
docs.contrast: The WCAG contrast ratio between two `#rrggbb` colours, 1 to 21. Body text wants 4.5, large or bold text 3.
docs.contrast_pairs: Every ink a `widget_theme` document's roles draw on the fill each draws it on, as `{ role, ink, fill, ratio, need }`. A role with no fill is read on the `ground` token; `need` is 3 for large or bold text and 4.5 otherwise.
docs.edit: Change a widget's value as the reader would, at the next tick, so it announces `value_changed`: a number for a slider or a number field, text for a text field, a dropdown's pick, a list's row or a tab, a colour for a swatch, a boolean for a fold. False for a disabled widget or a value its kind does not take.
docs.finish_loading: Say the load is through, which lets a held splash go once `splash_seconds` has also passed. The editor calls it once its shell has settled.
docs.focus_left: The same to the left, by `neighbour_left`.
docs.focus_next: Move focus to the next widget in scene order, wrapping past the last.
docs.focus_previous: Move focus to the previous widget in scene order, wrapping past the first.
docs.focus_right: The same to the right, by `neighbour_right`.
docs.focus_up: Move focus to the nearest widget above, as the up arrow does: the one the focused widget names in `neighbour_up`, else by where the widgets were drawn, round to the bottom past the top. What a stick or a d-pad's action calls.
docs.focused_widget: The widget node focus is on, or nil.
docs.free_picture: Let the picture `picture` named go, its texture with it; a widget still naming it draws its `alt_text`. False for a name no picture has.
docs.glyph: The character the icon font of the theme in force draws the glyph called `name` with, in the running project's own faces (the editor's, in the editor): for text that carries an icon among its words. Empty when the font has no glyph by that name. A widget's `icon`, a row's and a mark's take the name itself.
docs.height_class: How much height this screen has, as `ui::SHORT` or `ui::TALL`.
docs.natural_size: The width and height a `widget` node asks for before its container grows or shrinks it, as CSS's max-content, in design pixels: its content and padding, or what it or its role states, a container's from its children's. What a row of words weighs against its room. Zero until it has been laid out once; a hidden one keeps what it asked for when last shown.
docs.pasted_text: The text the last UI pass saw pasted, empty when it saw none: the platform clipboard is not readable on demand. The `pasted` event carries text no field took as it arrives.
docs.patch: What `patch` names written onto a widget node and remembered, so the next `write` compares against it: for a value that follows the node, what it leaves out is not asked about. False where nothing moved.
docs.picture: A picture from the bytes a script holds, PNG, JPEG, WebP, GIF or BMP, turned upright as its EXIF orientation says: the name an `image`'s `image` or a button's `image` draws it by, `picture:<n>`, held until `free_picture` lets it go. Nil for bytes that are no picture. What shows a photo from `device::pick_photo` before it is uploaded. A photo takes tens of milliseconds: call `picture_async` from a frame that has to stay smooth.
docs.picture_async: `picture` decoded on a worker: the id `task::wait` answers the picture's name on, or nil, once it is done. The picture is held from then on, waited on or not.
docs.pixels_per_design: How many of the window's own pixels a design pixel covers this frame: the UI scale, the display's scale and the reader's text size together. Divide `input::mouse_position()` by it for design pixels.
docs.request_repaint: Run the frame and its UI pass under `[window] low_processor`; call it every frame something on screen moves without input, such as while the scene plays. `after` seconds asks for one that far ahead instead.
docs.row_of: The row a `scroll`'s `scene_rows` built for its item at `index`, while it is built: nil for one out of view or not built yet.
docs.save_pasted_image: Write the image last pasted where no field took it, which the `image_pasted` event announced with its `{ width, height }`, to `path` as a PNG. Answers false when there is none, or it was written already.
docs.scale: The global UI scale: how many screen pixels a design pixel is drawn at, on top of the display's own.
docs.set_clipboard: Copy text to the system clipboard. The next UI pass hands it over, and asks for itself.
docs.set_focus: Put focus on a widget node. A node focus cannot activate is refused at the next draw.
docs.set_load_progress: Report how far a load is, zero to one. This is what holds `[application] splash` past its seconds, and what draws the bar under it.
docs.set_rows: Hand a `scroll`'s `scene_rows` their items: each row built is bound to the item at its place again, its script hearing it through `show(data)`, and the rows past the last are let go of. False for a node with no `scene_rows`.
docs.set_scale: Set the global UI scale, clamped to between 0.25 and 3.0. It is egui's zoom factor, so it grows every control and every font; `screen_size` already answers in the design pixels it leaves.
docs.set_theme: Put a theme in force over `[ui] theme` and `theme_dark`, for every widget and egui's own controls: a `widget_theme` file's path, or a theme document, with source colours under `colors` and sizes under `sizes`. What the document leaves out is derived from its sources. A root's own `theme` still dresses its subtree with that one, and nil goes back to the project's.
docs.tab_rect: Where a `tabs` page's own button in the strip was last drawn, as `{ x, y, width, height }` in design pixels; empty before the strip has drawn. `widget_rect` on the same node answers with the page body.
docs.takes_pointer_at: Whether the UI would take a press at this point, in design pixels, by the same layers as `wants_pointer`: what an editor asks of a point it is about to act on.
docs.theme_color: The colour the theme in force files under `name` in its `[colors]`, or a `#rrggbb` itself: for a script drawing in 2D in the theme's colours, read again when the system turns dark or light. Nil for a name the theme has no colour by.
docs.wants_keyboard: Whether a UI widget held keyboard focus when the last pass ended, so the game should leave key presses alone.
docs.wants_pointer: Whether the UI has the pointer or finger, so the game should leave it alone: what stops a tap on a HUD button also firing the shot behind it. A press is routed once, from the top: an open dialog, then a popup or window, then a widget that is not `interactive = false` or a seam between boxes, and the world last; it keeps that answer until the button comes up. False without a window.
docs.widget_rect: Where a `widget` node was last drawn, as `{ x, y, width, height }` in design pixels; empty until it has drawn once.
docs.width_class: How much width this screen has, as `ui::NARROW`, `ui::MEDIUM` or `ui::WIDE`. Read every frame: a rotation changes it. A run with no window answers `ui::WIDE`.
docs.window_size: The window's width and height, in design pixels; a headless run, and a script's `init` before the window opens, answer the `[window]` size the project states at the UI scale.
docs.write: Write each control table onto the widget node in its place, the lists side by side and in one call however long: each key to the component that holds it, `visible` to the node, and only what moved since the last write, a key an earlier write named and this one leaves out put back to its shape's default. A control carrying `controls` is a row; its children are the caller's to write. What names who hears it, `on_click`, `on_change`, `on_submit`, `target` and `data`, is never written. True when an earlier write differed.

modules.name: ui

modules.doc: A long-lived socket for text or binary frames. Events reach the node's `on_websocket_event` (or `on_event`) as a map with `socket` and `kind`: `open`, `message`, `binary`, `closed` or `error`, each an `EVENT_*` constant. An `error` carries its `reason`, and the HTTP `status` when a server refused the upgrade.

docs.close: Ask the connection to close, which still delivers a `closed` event with its `code`; false when it was already gone.
docs.connect: Open a connection and return the id `send_text`, `send_bytes` and `close` take, which `task.wait` resumes on with the `open` or `error` event; options are `on_event`, `compression` and `headers`. With no node, only a `task.wait` hears it.
docs.in_flight: How many sockets `connect` asked for still have their `open` or `error` to deliver; 0 means every one has woken its waiter, so a test's end waits with `while websocket::in_flight() > 0 { await task::frames(1); }`.
docs.send_bytes: Queue a binary frame on the connection; false when it is already gone.
docs.send_text: Queue a text frame on the connection; false when it is already gone.
docs.state: Where the connection is: `connecting`, `open`, `closing` or `closed`, each a `STATE_*` constant.

modules.name: websocket

modules.doc: The OS window and the display under it: mode, cursor, app icon, keep-awake, the safe area and the refresh rate.

docs.refresh_rate: Frames per second the display refreshes at, as measured over the last frames; 60 with no window.
docs.safe_area: The display's insets in pixels, `{ left, top, right, bottom }`: what a notch or a home bar covers, read once per frame and recorded. Zero on a desktop.
docs.set_app_icon: Set the application icon, the dock or taskbar one, from a PNG or an SVG in the project. `opts.plate` colours the disc a macOS dock icon sits on, white by default. Replaces `[application] icon` for the run.
docs.set_cursor_grab: Confine the cursor to the window, for FPS-style mouse look.
docs.set_cursor_hidden: Hide or show the mouse cursor over the window.
docs.set_keep_awake: Keep the screen from dimming while the game runs: a page takes a wake lock, a phone its equivalent, a desktop needs nothing.
docs.set_window_mode: `windowed`, `maximized`, `fullscreen` (borderless) or `exclusive` (the monitor's largest video mode): the same choice as `[window] mode`.

modules.name: window

node_events: the child; freed, it is still readable in this node's own hook
the name it had; `name()` says the new one
the parent it left; `parent()` says the new one
said_events: Lines were logged since the last frame.
A file the asset cache holds was reloaded or declared stale.
the paths, as a list; empty when the watcher lost count
A burst of file writes under the project, or under a directory `engine::watch` follows, has ended.
A script stopped, or stopped somewhere else.
The script the debugger last said was stopped went on.
the state playback moved to, a `replay::STATE_*` constant
A recording was loaded, played, paused, sought, ran out or was unloaded.
a list of `{ node, kind, .. }` maps
A write changed the scene since the last frame; heard from a node, the entries under it alone.

The player signed out in the OS or signed in as someone else, a notification or a push was tapped (`notification_opened`) or arrived while the game was in front (`notification_received`, `push_received`), a link opened the game (`url_opened`, with its `url`; the one it was launched with too), the OS replaced the push token (`push_token_changed`), or a purchase landed with nobody asking (`transaction`).
Something nobody asked for arrived: an invite, an iCloud change. A link that opened the game, a push and its token are `platform_event`.
the message, as the parent frame posted it
The page's parent frame posted a message.
the progress, with the `request` it belongs to
A download or a long body moved on.
a map whose `kind` is an `EVENT_*` constant
A match had something to say.
The camera a frame was drawn with moved, or the window it was drawn into did.
A screenshot came to no file.
Steam said something: the map's `kind` is the callback's name, a `steam::EVENT_*` constant, beside its fields.
Text was pasted where no field took it.
An image was pasted where no field took it.
where the pointer is in window pixels, `[x, y]`
A button went down anywhere, the UI included.
A button came up anywhere, the UI included.
`{ scale, x, y, pan_x, pan_y }`, `scale` zero for a pan alone
the files' paths, as a list
Files were dropped on the window.

spec.help: The game's name, used for its window title and its data directory.
The scene a run opens with.

The Balaur build the project is made with, as `balaur --version` names it: a release (`v0.2.0-alpha.1`) or a nightly (`nightly-577592f`). Written when a project is made and by `balaur pin`; a run or an export on another build says so, and the Forge builds the project on it. Empty names none.
Where a shipped game may read its bytes from. Only bites once packed; a dev run always reads the source tree.
A project-relative picture shown over the first frames, on every target. Empty shows none.
How long the splash stays, in seconds of engine time, and the least it stays when a script is reporting a load through `ui.set_load_progress`.

Project paths that are not the game's, as globs: `art/wip/**`, `**/*.blend1`. The asset index skips them and a pack leaves them out; a target's override is its export's alone, `[override.web.application] ignore`.

A project-relative square picture, a PNG or an SVG, that every export writes as that platform's app icon, and the window shows while the game runs. 1024 pixels is what a store asks for. Empty: an iOS, Android or macOS app shows Balaur's.
The icon's form for a dark system: the dark appearance on iOS and macOS, the favicon a dark browser shows, and the window icon while `dark_mode()` is true.
A single-colour form, white on transparency, that iOS and macOS tint and Android 13 draws in the themed launcher.
Logical width. The backing store is this times the display's scale, which is what the render targets are sized from.
Logical height.

How the window opens: at its size, maximized, borderless over the whole screen, or exclusive, which takes the monitor's largest video mode. window.set_window_mode changes it later through the same state.
Which way up a phone may hold the game. Written into the export's own manifest, since a device decides this before the game runs.
Present in step with the display.
Samples per pixel. 1 is off and 4 is the only other count the renderer offers; it costs two render targets of four samples each.
The most frames a second the loop draws. Zero paces it against the tick instead, which is what vsync already does on a display that runs at the tick rate.

Run a frame only while something asks for one: input, ui.request_repaint, a log line, a changed file, work finished on another thread, or simulation still under way. That is a timer or a task wait counting, a clip or a tween playing, a body awake, particles alive, a sound that will end, a replay or a match. With none of them the loop sleeps. What a tool or an app of still screens wants; a game that moves every frame gains nothing from it.

Let a character no face of the project has a glyph for draw in the face the operating system picks for it, instead of tofu. A worker reads every font on the machine once, after the first frame, so a game that only draws what it vendors can turn it off.
A project-relative `widget_theme` every widget and egui's own controls start from, as Godot's project theme is. A widget that names its own `theme` still dresses its subtree with that one.
The theme's form for a dark system, worn while `dark_mode()` is true. `ui.set_theme` goes over both.

How large the game's own UI is drawn, as egui's zoom factor: every control and every font together, on top of the display's own scale. A phone usually wants more than a desktop, which is what `[override.mobile.ui] scale` is for. `ui.set_scale` changes it later.
Multiply the scale by the size the reader asked their system for. Off for a game whose layout cannot give text more room.
Under this many design pixels of width a layout reads `narrow`: one column, one panel at a time. Android's own line between its compact and medium window classes.
From this many design pixels of width a layout reads `wide` and may spread out. Between the two lines it reads `medium`.
Under this many design pixels of height a layout reads `short`, which is a phone on its side.

The project's own class words, beside the screen's (`touch`, `pointer`, `short`, `tall`, `narrow`, `medium`, `wide`), in the order their tables override: later wins. A widget's `classes` puts one in force for itself and what it lays out, a container's `fit` puts them in force by measuring, and a theme's role or a scene's widget answers one with a table of that name, as it answers `narrow`. A table named for a word declared nowhere is refused.

How far a finger travels on a `scroll` before it scrolls, in design pixels, so a tap that wobbles stays a tap on what it landed on: Android's touch slop, Godot's `scroll_deadzone` for every scroll. A scroll's own `scroll_deadzone` goes over it; 0 scrolls at once.
How many fixed steps a second the simulation takes, the same on every platform: a recording replays and a match steps at one rate. Sixty is the rate the cross-platform digest job runs.
`balaur check` fails on a warning as well as an error, for this project on every run.
The locale a fresh run starts in. Empty starts in the system's language where the project ships it, else in `fallback`.
Where a key missing from the current locale is looked for next.

The languages, or whole locales like `pt_BR`, written right to left. A UI in one lays out mirrored: rows run from the right, start and end swap, and an icon the theme lists under `[icons] mirrored` turns round.
Put delay, jitter and packet loss on every multiplayer link, to test rollback against a link that misbehaves.
Ticks every payload waits before delivery. Nine is about 150 ms at 60 Hz.
Extra ticks drawn per payload. Jitter is what reorders a stream.
The fraction of datagrams dropped. Datagrams only: losing a reliable payload would break the transport's contract.
Between texels. Nearest is what keeps pixel art crisp when it is magnified.
What a coordinate past the edge reads. Mirror tiles without a seam.
Build the smaller copies a texture drawn small samples, which stops it shimmering. A picture on a 3D surface builds them unless this says or its filter is nearest.
Samples per fetch on a surface seen edge-on. Needs every filter linear.
Scale colour by alpha at upload, so a soft edge blends with no dark fringe. 2D nodes only.
Off for a normal map or a mask, which carry data rather than colour.
Spread the edge colour into fully transparent texels, so a linear filter never samples a dark or white fringe. Colour sampled linearly only.
Texture pixels to one world unit, for every sprite whose own pixels_per_unit is 0. A pixel-art project sets its tile size here once.
Every sound's own level, multiplied into each play of it. A file's sidecar sets its own.
Loop every sound wherever it is played. A music folder usually sets this per file instead.
Mix every WAV to one channel at export, which halves a stereo file. A sound played from a place in the world is heard mono anyway.
The highest sample rate a WAV ships at, in Hz; 0 keeps each file's own. 22050 is plenty for most effects. Set it per target to ship a phone less.
Trim the padding an encoder adds to a compressed file, where the file records it, so files queued back to back play without a gap.
How large a project face's glyphs are drawn and spaced, in the UI and in world text.
Snap a face's outlines to the pixel grid. Off for a smooth face drawn large.
Smooth glyph edges. Off draws each pixel fully on or off, for a pixel face at its own size; egui's own text and magnified world text stay smooth.
A model file's units to the scene's: 0.01 for files modelled in centimetres. A skinned mesh is left as authored.
How many simpler copies of every rigid model to build at load, each with half the triangles of the one before.
The camera distance, in world units, at which the first simpler copy takes over; each further one takes over at twice it.
Write each run's log to logs/run.log in the user data directory, so a crash leaves its last lines behind.
How many earlier runs' logs stay beside it, as run.1.log and on.
The output device, by a name `audio.devices()` lists. Empty, or a device that is not connected, opens the system's default.
Output channels. 0 takes the device's own.
Output sample rate. 0 takes the device's own.
Frames per output buffer. Fewer answers sooner and risks dropouts; 0 takes 50 ms of frames, rodio's default.
The bit depth the whole mix is dithered to before the device. 0 is off; a build without the `dither` feature leaves the mix alone.
The server's web OAuth client id (`….apps.googleusercontent.com`), which an id token is issued for. Not a secret. Empty: `google.sign_in` answers `unsupported`.
Seconds for a whole request, when the call names none.
Requests running at once; the rest wait their turn.
A finger also moves the mouse, so every widget written against a pointer works on a phone.
The mouse also reports a finger, so touch code runs on a desktop. Off by default: a game reading both would see one press twice.
How far a finger travels before a lift counts as a swipe, in design pixels.
How long a finger holds before it counts as a long press.
How far a held finger may wander and still be holding, in design pixels.
Fraction of a stick's or a trigger's travel that reads zero, on every pad; the rest is rescaled so the first live reading is near zero.
Pressure at which a pad button or trigger goes down.
Pressure below which a down pad button comes up again; at most gamepad_press.
Seconds a pad button is held before gamepad_repeated first fires again.
Seconds between gamepad_repeated firings after the delay.
Extra pad layouts in SDL's mapping format, one per entry, for a pad SDL's database does not know. Loaded when the process first reads pads.
What a host listens with: QUIC datagrams, or a websocket where UDP is blocked.
Where a host listens. 0.0.0.0 lets other machines in; port 0 takes any free one.
How many slots fill before a match starts on its own; 0 waits for the host's `start`.
The scene a match loads on every machine; empty for the main scene.
Snapshots kept for rollback: how many ticks late an input can still be answered.
Seconds a join may take, and a link may go silent, before it is dropped.
How far two colliders may drift, scaled by length_unit, before their contacts are worked out again rather than reused.
How the 3D solver treats friction: one cone per four contacts and a twist, or one per contact, slower and closer. A multibody always uses one per contact.
The 3D world's gravity, in units per second squared: the value physics3d.set_gravity writes and physics3d.gravity reads.
The 2D world's gravity, in units per second squared: the value physics2d.set_gravity writes and physics2d.gravity reads.
Solver iterations per step. More is stabler and slower; every value here changes results, so a recording only replays against the same numbers.
Substeps for continuous collision detection, which stops a fast body tunnelling through a thin one.
How many of the game's units make a metre. A pixel game sets this rather than scaling every body.
Group contacts before solving them.
Reuse contact state between steps.
How far a body may sink into another before the solver pushes back.
A cap on how fast the solver may push overlapping bodies apart.
How far ahead contacts are predicted.

Iterations spent pushing overlapping bodies apart rather than solving velocities.

How much of the last step's impulses the solver starts from.

Solve friction in the bias pass, which is stabler at the cost of a little drift.

Side of the shadow map, in texels.

Shadow-map layers every casting light shares: a spot light takes one, a directional one a layer per cascade and a point one six. A light past the budget lights without a shadow. Each layer costs `shadow_resolution` squared times eight bytes.
How many layers of glass seen through glass are drawn; each costs another snapshot of the scene and another glass pass.
Clusters the many-light pass cuts the view into, across x, across y and along depth, each 1 to 128. Finer culls tighter and costs memory. Not drawn on WebGL2, which has no compute.
Lights one cluster records; past it a dense cluster drops lights. The renderer lowers it to fit the device's largest storage buffer.
Side of each cube face a `reflection_probe` captures, and the width of every probe map, which all probes share. A change clears every map and captures the probes again.
Offer permessage-deflate on every connection; the server decides whether frames are compressed.

The runtime a game is put on. 2d and 3d carry one physics world each and bare carries neither, so each weighs less than full, and auto takes the smallest the scenes and scripts fit, or the full one where only that is on hand; name one where a script builds a component's name at run time. A server target keeps its own. Per target through that target's override.
A project-relative directory; each target gets a subdirectory of it. Empty exports where the command stands.
Drop an asset no scene, script or include glob names. Off by default: a script may compute a path this cannot see, and losing an asset is worse than shipping one.
Names this build answers to besides its platform's, such as demo or store. An override or an asset variant may be written for any of them; per target, set it under that target's override.
Globs an export includes whatever else it decides, for the paths a script builds at run time.
How an image is re-encoded on the way into the pack, kept only where it comes out smaller. Every mode keeps the size; quantized is the one that does not keep the pixels.
imagequant's quality target, which image_recode = "quantized" reads and every other mode ignores.

The longest side an image ships at, in pixels; 0 keeps every size. Set it per target to ship a phone a smaller art set. Pixel art and bitmap font pages are never capped, and a sprite keeps the size it was drawn at.
Whether a font is cut down to the characters the project's scenes and scripts name.
Code points a subset font keeps beyond the ones found in the project, as first-last hex ranges ("0020-00FF"), for text from a server or typed by a player.
Faces that ship whole however font_recode is set, as globs: the one a text field draws with cannot be subset to the characters this project happens to contain.
How uncompressed audio is re-encoded, kept only where it comes out smaller. flac keeps every sample; vorbis does not.
libvorbis's quality, which audio_recode = "vorbis" reads and every other mode ignores.

Scenes, as globs, whose assets a web export ships in a second file the page fetches after the game starts. A switch to one waits until that file has arrived; no other scene may name what only these do.

Ship the scripts as native code, built from their C with Xcode for an Apple target or clang and lld for any. auto falls back to the target's engine when no compiler is found, on fails the export instead, off never builds it. Per target through that target's override.
The identifier Play resolves an OAuth client, a licence and an update against. Required to export.
The name under the icon. Empty means [application] name.
versionName: what a player is shown. Required to export.
versionCode: what Play orders updates by, and the only one it reads. Required to export; 0 is unset.
The API floor. 0 defers to the template's own, which is what its libraries were built against.
The API this game says it was written for. Google Play takes a new app or an update only at 36 or later.
Which of the template's ABIs the export keeps. None named means every one it carries, so a game that says nothing ships everywhere.
A project-relative keystore. Without one an export needs --sign debug, which installs on a device and ships nowhere.
Which key in that keystore signs.
Where bundletool.jar is. Empty looks at BALAUR_ANDROID_BUNDLETOOL and then beside the SDK; Google ships it on its own, not in the SDK.
The permissions the manifest declares: INTERNET for android.permission.INTERNET, or a whole name. Without INTERNET no socket opens; a game that never goes online writes permissions = [].

The custom URL schemes that open the game, each an intent filter: the scheme a platform.web_sign_in page ends on (com.studio.game for com.studio.game:/done), which its Custom Tab answers with. Any other link on one arrives as url_opened on platform_event.

The Google services the game uses, each shipping its Google libraries: play-games for platform.* on Play Games, in-app-purchase for Play Billing, in-app-review for device.request_review, firebase-messaging for platform.register_for_push. None named ships no Google library.
The Play Games project id Play Console shows under Play Games Services, all digits. Required with play-games.

The project-relative google-services.json the Firebase console hands out, holding this application_id's app. Required with firebase-messaging, whose project, app id, API key and sender id it writes as the string resources Firebase starts from. The file itself stays out of the game's pack.

A project-relative square picture with transparency, the small icon Android draws in the status bar for the game's notifications, local and pushed. Only its alpha is read: the export writes it white at each density. Empty shows the system's reminder icon.
The identifier registered in App Store Connect. Required to export.
The ten-character team identifier. Nothing expands it, so an entitlement carrying the prefix needs the real value.
The name under the icon. Empty means [application] name.
CFBundleShortVersionString: what a player is shown. Required to export.
CFBundleVersion: what the store orders uploads by. Required to export.
MinimumOSVersion on iOS. A plist may not claim less than the binary was built for.
LSMinimumSystemVersion on macOS.
LSApplicationCategoryType, macOS only, which the Mac App Store requires: e.g. public.app-category.education.

What the bundle declares it uses. Each writes its own entitlement and its own minimum OS. push-notifications writes aps-environment: development for a build signed by a development identity or none, production for a distribution one.
Developer ID Application: … for a download, Apple Distribution: … for the Mac App Store. The password behind it is read from the environment, never from here.
The identity a Mac App Store .pkg is signed with, 3rd Party Mac Developer Installer: …. Empty derives it from an Apple Distribution macos_identity.

A project-relative .provisionprofile, the Developer ID or Mac App Store profile macos_identity goes with, embedded as Contents/embedded.provisionprofile. A signed Mac build needs one for sign-in-with-apple, game-center, icloud-kv or push-notifications; a capability the profile does not grant (a Developer ID profile has no Sign in with Apple) is left out of the Mac build, which answers unsupported for it.
Submit to Apple's notary service after signing, and staple the ticket.
The identity an iOS build is signed with.
A project-relative .mobileprovision, copied into the bundle. The export refuses one that does not grant what the capabilities write.

The custom URL schemes that open the game, as CFBundleURLTypes on iOS and a Mac: a link on one arrives as url_opened on platform_event. Named by [android] schemes' rule: lowercase, a letter first, then letters, digits, +, - or ., and not http or https.

com.apple.developer.associated-domains, each as Apple writes it (applinks:game.studio.com): a universal link to one opens the game, arriving as url_opened. Granted by the provisioning profile only, which the export checks, and the domain serves apple-app-site-association naming the app.
A project-relative .pfx, or an Azure Trusted Signing metadata file when the key lives in a cloud HSM.
The timestamp authority a Windows signature is countersigned by.

The app id Steamworks gave the game; 0 is unset. `balaur export --steam`, which needs it, ships Valve's steam_api beside the game; with --dev it also writes the id to steam_appid.txt, so the game starts without the Steam client. An export without --steam ships no Valve file.
